metric.why: Distributed AI training is unusually intolerant of network degradation; a lossy fabric shows up as wasted GPU-hours before it shows up as an outage.
metric.metric: Network latency, packet loss, and bandwidth
metric.definition: Continuous measurement of round-trip latency, loss rate, and utilization on the facility's internal fabric and external transit.

reading.body:
Network latency, packet loss, and bandwidth degradation directly waste GPU-hours in distributed AI training before they register as facility outages, making continuous fabric monitoring essential operational data.

AI training at scale distributes computation across many GPUs, often in different buildings or regions. The network connecting them becomes part of the compute path itself. A single millisecond of added latency or a small percentage of dropped packets forces GPUs to idle while waiting for data, turning expensive hardware into dead weight. This waste compounds across thousands of devices and weeks of training runs, accumulating costs that facility managers cannot see in conventional uptime metrics.

Data centers track this through continuous measurement of round-trip latency, loss rate, and utilization on both internal fabrics and external transit links. The metric differs from SLA uptime compliance or generator runtime because those measure whether the lights stay on. This measures whether the lights are actually lighting useful work. A facility can be technically "up" while losing 2 percent of packets, and that facility is quietly burning money on wasted training cycles.

The data does not specify what latency or loss thresholds trigger action, how measurements are aggregated across multi-building campuses, or how this monitoring informs procurement and layout decisions. It identifies what matters to measure without defining what good looks like.
